title: A small fish
hookLine: govern a great country as you'd cook a small fish, without too much poking (Tao Te Ching 60)

lines: A FISH IN A HOT PAN.
A COUNTRY IN THE SAME PAN.
cards: A small fish is sizzling in a pan. Someone stands over it with a spatula and can't leave it alone. Lift the edge, check the color, nudge it, flip it, flip it back.

By the time it's cooked, it's in flakes all over the pan, and there isn't much fish left to serve. Chapter sixty of the Tao Te Ching sets that kitchen scene right next to a far bigger job: running a country.
It sounds like a joke. It isn't.

teach.h: A GREAT STATE, A SMALL FISH.
teach.b: First, the line itself. In James Legge's translation, chapter sixty opens: "Governing a great state is like cooking small fish." That's the whole instruction; it leaves the cook to work out the how.
Second, why a small fish. A thick cut of meat can take some handling, but a small fish is delicate.

An old commentary, the one tradition credits to Heshang Gong, reads it this way: don't dare to stir it, or it falls apart. So the skill is mostly restraint: get the heat right, put it in, let it cook.

teach.h: EVERY TURN BREAKS IT A LITTLE.
teach.b: A country, in this picture, is fragile in the same way, and every new order, every shake-up, every fresh rule turns the fish over once more. Third, the stranger second half.

When the world is ruled by the Tao, the chapter says, the spirits of the dead lose their power to harm. Not that they have no power, it adds, but that it doesn't hurt people. And the sage doesn't hurt people either.

When neither side does harm, their goodness flows together. Some readers hear old beliefs about ghosts; some hear that a calm, unmeddling order leaves less room for dread of any kind. The text doesn't settle it.

Fourth, the small fish in daily life: an inbox, a team, a teenager's homework, a sourdough starter, a friendship that went quiet. The pull is to keep turning it: one more text, one more check, one more tweak to the plan.
Chapter sixty leaves a plain kitchen question on the counter.
Is this still cooking, or is it just poking?

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter sixty as advice for anyone in charge of something fragile: set it up well, then hold back from constant meddling.

o: a ruler's picture: handle a great state lightly
a sign of the poor food that peasants lived on
a gift offered to calm the spirits of the dead

s: chapter sixty gives detailed rules for governing
it gives one kitchen picture and leaves the cook to work out the rest.
the chapter says the spirits have no power at all
it says their power doesn't hurt people, not that they have none.
the chapter says the sage doesn't hurt people
and when neither the spirits nor the sage do harm, their goodness flows together.

games.q: a small fish is starting to sizzle in your pan. what do you do?
o: flip it to check the underside.
leave it alone and let it cook.
games.why: chapter sixty compares ruling a great state to cooking small fish, and an old commentary reads it: don't stir it, or it falls apart.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been turning over and over: a message you keep rereading, a plan you keep adjusting, a person you keep checking on.
For these two minutes, set the spatula down; the fish is in the pan, and the heat is on. If the urge to check comes back, let it drift off like steam rising from the pan.

wordCard.voice: A small fish. In chapter sixty, ruling a great state is like cooking one: handle it lightly, or it falls apart. Today's word.
